claim: Nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB)-mediated transcription is an important mediator for cellular responses to DNA damage.
source: Nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB)-mediated transcription is an important mediator for cellular responses to DNA damage.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Genotoxic agents trigger a 'nuclear-to-cytoplasmic' NF-κB activation signaling pathway.
source: Genotoxic agents trigger a 'nuclear-to-cytoplasmic' NF-κB activation signaling pathway
evidence: This is established knowledge about the NF-κB activation mechanism.

claim: The early nuclear signaling cascade linking DNA damage and NF-κB activation is poorly understood.
source: however, the early nuclear signaling cascade linking DNA damage and NF-κB activation is poorly understood.
evidence: This statement reflects the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Sam68/KHDRBS1 is a key NF-κB regulator in genotoxic stress-initiated signaling pathway.
source: Here we report that Src-associated-substrate-during-mitosis-of-68kDa/KH domain containing, RNA binding, signal transduction associated 1 (Sam68/KHDRBS1) is a key NF-κB regulator in genotoxic stress-initiated signaling pathway.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Sam68 deficiency abolishes DNA damage-stimulated polymers of ADP-ribose (PAR) production.
source: Sam68 deficiency abolishes DNA damage-stimulated polymers of ADP-ribose (PAR) production and the PAR-dependent NF-κB transactivation of anti-apoptotic genes.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 and related experiments.

claim: Sam68 deficiency abolishes PAR-dependent NF-κB transactivation of anti-apoptotic genes.
source: Sam68 deficiency abolishes DNA damage-stimulated polymers of ADP-ribose (PAR) production and the PAR-dependent NF-κB transactivation of anti-apoptotic genes.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Sam68 deleted cells are hypersensitive to genotoxicity caused by DNA damaging agents.
source: Sam68 deleted cells are hypersensitive to genotoxicity caused by DNA damaging agents.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Upregulated Sam68 coincides with elevated PAR production in human and mouse colon cancer.
source: Upregulated Sam68 coincides with elevated PAR production and NF-κB-mediated anti-apoptotic transcription in human and mouse colon cancer.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Upregulated Sam68 coincides with elevated NF-κB-mediated anti-apoptotic transcription in human and mouse colon cancer.
source: Upregulated Sam68 coincides with elevated PAR production and NF-κB-mediated anti-apoptotic transcription in human and mouse colon cancer.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Knockdown of Sam68 sensitizes human colon cancer cells to genotoxic stress-induced apoptosis.
source: Knockdown of Sam68 sensitizes human colon cancer cells to genotoxic stress-induced apoptosis and genetic deletion of Sam68 dampens colon tumor burden in mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Genetic deletion of Sam68 dampens colon tumor burden in mice.
source: Knockdown of Sam68 sensitizes human colon cancer cells to genotoxic stress-induced apoptosis and genetic deletion of Sam68 dampens colon tumor burden in mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: NF-κB responds to genotoxic threats via the activation of the inhibitor of NF-κB kinase (IKK) and NF-κB liberation from IκB proteins.
source: NF-κB responds to genotoxic threats (e.g. DNA damaging agents and γ-irradiation) via the activation of the inhibitor of NF-κB kinase (IKK) and NF-κB liberation from IκB proteins, similar to the canonical pathway activated by external stimuli (Janssens et al., 2005; Perkins, 2007; Scheidereit, 2006; Wu and Miyamoto, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: NF-κB signaling pathway has emerged as an important mediator for cellular responses to DNA damage.
source: NF-κB signaling pathway has emerged as an important mediator for cellular responses to DNA damage, in particular NF-κB-conferred anti-apoptotic transcription facilitates the cell 'escape' from the lethal effects of DNA damage (Janssens et al., 2005; Perkins, 2007; Scheidereit, 2006; Wu and Miyamoto, 2007)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: NF-κB-conferred anti-apoptotic transcription facilitates the cell 'escape' from the lethal effects of DNA damage.
source: in particular NF-κB-conferred anti-apoptotic transcription facilitates the cell 'escape' from the lethal effects of DNA damage (Janssens et al., 2005; Perkins, 2007; Scheidereit, 2006; Wu and Miyamoto, 2007)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: NF-κB initiates cell cycle checkpoint control to promote cellular recovery from damage.
source: and initiates cell cycle checkpoint control to promote cellular recovery from damage (McCool and Miyamoto, 2012; Miyamoto, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: ATM is a crucial regulator of the genotoxic stress-activated NF-κB signaling pathway.
source: Besides ataxia telangiectasia mutated (ATM) and IKKγ, two known crucial regulators of the genotoxic stress-activated NF-κB signaling pathway (Li et al., 2001; Piret et al., 1999)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: IKKγ is a crucial regulator of the genotoxic stress-activated NF-κB signaling pathway.
source: Besides ataxia telangiectasia mutated (ATM) and IKKγ, two known crucial regulators of the genotoxic stress-activated NF-κB signaling pathway (Li et al., 2001; Piret et al., 1999)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: PARP1 is indispensable for the signaling cascade that links nuclear DNA damage recognition to cytoplasmic IKK activation.
source: poly (ADP-ribose) polymerase 1 (PARP1) was recently revealed to be indispensable for the signaling cascade that links nuclear DNA damage recognition to cytoplasmic IKK activation (Stilmann et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Sequential post-translational modifications, including phosphorylation, ubiquitination and SUMOylation, of signaling regulators are critical for NF-κB activation following DNA damage.
source: Sequential post-translational modifications, including phosphorylation, ubiquitination and SUMOylation, of these signaling regulators are critical for NF-κB activation following DNA damage (Huang et al., 2003; Mabb et al., 2006; Wu et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: PARP1-catalyzed poly (ADP-ribosyl)ation (PARylation) has emerged as a vital means for rapid assembly of the signaling complexes that are critical for DNA damage-initiated NF-κB activation.
source: in particular, PARP1-catalyzed poly (ADP-ribosyl)ation (PARylation) has emerged as a vital means for rapid assembly of the signaling complexes that are critical for DNA damage-initiated NF-κB activation (Mabb et al., 2006; Stilmann et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Sam68 is an RNA-binding protein that preferentially resides in the nucleus.
source: Sam68 (Src-associated substrate during mitosis of 68 kDa, also named KH domain containing, RNA binding, signal transduction associated 1 [KHDRBS1], and encoded by KHDRBS1 gene), an RNA-binding protein that preferentially resides in the nucleus, plays versatile functions in an increasing number of cellular processes (Bielli et al., 2011; Cheung et al., 2007; Fu et al., 2013; Glisovic et al., 2008; Henao-Mejia et al., 2009; Huot et al., 2012; Iijima et al., 2011; Lukong and Richard, 2003; Matter et al., 2002; Paronetto et al., 2009; Rajan et al., 2008a, 2008b; Ramakrishnan and Baltimore, 2011; Richard, 2010; Sette, 2010; Yang et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Sam68 plays versatile functions in an increasing number of cellular processes.
source: Sam68 (Src-associated substrate during mitosis of 68 kDa, also named KH domain containing, RNA binding, signal transduction associated 1 [KHDRBS1], and encoded by KHDRBS1 gene), an RNA-binding protein that preferentially resides in the nucleus, plays versatile functions in an increasing number of cellular processes (Bielli et al., 2011; Cheung et al., 2007; Fu et al., 2013; Glisovic et al., 2008; Henao-Mejia et al., 2009; Huot et al., 2012; Iijima et al., 2011; Lukong and Richard, 2003; Matter et al., 2002; Paronetto et al., 2009; Rajan et al., 2008a, 2008b; Ramakrishnan and Baltimore, 2011; Richard, 2010; Sette, 2010; Yang et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Sam68 is capable of binding single- and double-stranded DNA in addition to RNA through its KH domain.
source: Through its KH (heteronuclear ribonucleoprotein particle K homology) domain, Sam68 is capable of binding single- and double-stranded DNA in addition to RNA (Lukong and Richard, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Sam68 was identified as a PAR-binding protein in alkylating agent treated cells.
source: Of note, Sam68 was identified as a PAR-binding protein in alkylating agent treated cells (Gagne et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Sam68 is a putative substrate of ATM, ATR, and DNA-PK.
source: and a putative substrate of ATM, ATM and Rad3-related (ATR), and DNA-dependent protein kinase (DNA-PK) (Beli et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Aberrant expression of Sam68 has been acknowledged in multiple cancers.
source: Moreover, aberrant expression of Sam68 has been acknowledged in multiple cancers and elevated Sam68 expression correlates with tumor progression and poor prognosis in cancer patients (Chen et al., 2012; Liao et al., 2013; Song et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Elevated Sam68 expression correlates with tumor progression and poor prognosis in cancer patients.
source: Moreover, aberrant expression of Sam68 has been acknowledged in multiple cancers and elevated Sam68 expression correlates with tumor progression and poor prognosis in cancer patients (Chen et al., 2012; Liao et al., 2013; Song et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Overexpression of Sam68 has been proposed as a prognostic marker.
source: Overexpression of Sam68 has been proposed as a prognostic marker (Chen et al., 2012; Liao et al., 2013; Song et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The precise function of Sam68 in cancer development and survival remains obscure.
source: however, the precise function of Sam68 in cancer development and survival remains obscure.
evidence: This statement reflects the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Camptothecin (CPT) stimulated a rapid degradation of IκBα in a dose- and time-dependent manner in wild-type MEFs.
source: As expected, Camptothecin (CPT), a DNA-damaging chemical that inhibits DNA topoisomerase I (Stilmann et al., 2009), stimulated a rapid degradation of IκBα, a prerequisite for NF-κB liberation and transactivation, in a dose- and time-dependent manner in wild-type MEFs (Figure 1A–B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A-B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: DNA damage-induced IκBα degradation was remarkably attenuated in Sam68 KO MEFs.
source: In contrast, DNA damage-induced IκBα degradation was remarkably attenuated in Sam68 KO MEFs (Figure 1A–B)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A-B.

claim: DNA damage-induced IκBα degradation was remarkably attenuated in MEFs without PARP1.
source: and MEFs without poly(ADP-ribose)polymerase 1 (PARP1) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), a recently identified key nuclear regulator of DNA damage-induced NF-κB activation (Stilmann et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and citation to previous literature.

claim: CPT treatment triggered remarkable nuclear translocation of NF-κB in wild-type MEFs.
source: Moreover, CPT treatment triggered remarkable nuclear translocation of NF-κB in wild-type MEFs (Figure 1C)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Nuclear extracts from CPT-treated wild-type MEFs formed high-affinity binding complexes with immunoglobin (Ig) κB double-stranded DNA.
source: additionally, the derived nuclear extracts formed high-affinity binding complexes with immunoglobin (Ig) κB double-stranded DNA, which was further confirmed by cold oligonucleotide competition and super shift assays (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: NF-κB nuclear accumulation and binding capacity to Ig κB DNA were almost abolished in the CPT-stimulated Sam68 KO MEFs.
source: In striking contrast, NF-κB nuclear accumulation and binding capacity to Ig κB DNA were almost abolished in the CPT-stimulated Sam68 KO MEFs (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C-D.

claim: CPT-triggered IκBα degradation was substantially reduced in Sam68-specific siRNA-expressing wild-type MEFs.
source: CPT-triggered IκBα degradation was substantially reduced in Sam68-specific siRNA-expressing wild-type MEFs, compared to scrambled non-specific siRNA-transfected cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Ectopic expression of GFP tagged Sam68 markedly restored CPT-induced IκBα degradation in Sam68 KO MEFs.
source: whereas ectopic expression of green fluorescent protein (GFP) tagged Sam68, but not GFP alone, markedly restored CPT-induced IκBα degradation in Sam68 KO MEFs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D-E.

claim: Sam68 is an almost strictly nuclear protein.
source: Sam68 is an almost strictly nuclear protein; its nuclear import is conferred by a nuclear localization signal (NLS) in the C-terminus (Fu et al., 2013; Ishidate et al., 1997; Lukong and Richard, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Sam68's nuclear import is conferred by a nuclear localization signal (NLS) in the C-terminus.
source: Sam68 is an almost strictly nuclear protein; its nuclear import is conferred by a nuclear localization signal (NLS) in the C-terminus (Fu et al., 2013; Ishidate et al., 1997; Lukong and Richard, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The ΔC (deletion of C-terminal NLS) mutant of Sam68 switches its preferred subcellular localization to the cytoplasm.
source: Consistently, the ΔC (deletion of C-terminal NLS) mutant of Sam68 switches its preferred subcellular localization to the cytoplasm, in contrast to the strict nuclear accumulation observed in wild-type Sam68 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Sam68 KO MEFs reconstituted with wild-type Sam68 displayed restored CPT-triggered NF-κB activation signaling.
source: Sam68 KO MEFs reconstituted with wild-type Sam68, but not GFP control, displayed restored CPT-triggered NF-κB activation signaling including IκBα degradation, phosphorylation of p65, and p65 nuclear accumulation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E-F.

claim: Supplementing with the Sam68 (ΔC) mutant failed to restore CPT-triggered IκBα degradation.
source: In contrast, supplementing with the Sam68 (ΔC) mutant failed to restore CPT-triggered IκBα degradation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The Sam68 nuclear function is indispensable for DNA damage-initiated NF-κB activation.
source: which indicates an indispensable role of the Sam68 nuclear function in DNA damage-initiated NF-κB activation.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results showing that the cytoplasmic mutant cannot rescue NF-κB activation.

claim: CPT treatment-induced SUMOylation of IKKγ was substantially attenuated in Sam68 KO MEFs.
source: Indeed, CPT treatment-induced SUMOylation of IKKγ, a pivotal post-translational modification on IKKγ in the nucleus that subsequently leads to activation of IKKβ and liberation of NF-κB in the cytoplasm (Huang et al., 2003; Mabb et al., 2006), was substantially attenuated in Sam68 KO MEFs in comparison to wild-type controls (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and citations to previous literature.

claim: SUMOylation of IKKγ is a pivotal post-translational modification in the nucleus that subsequently leads to activation of IKKβ and liberation of NF-κB in the cytoplasm.
source: CPT treatment-induced SUMOylation of IKKγ, a pivotal post-translational modification on IKKγ in the nucleus that subsequently leads to activation of IKKβ and liberation of NF-κB in the cytoplasm (Huang et al., 2003; Mabb et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Assembly of the PARP1-IKKγ signal complex is a prerequisite for cytoplasmic NF-κB activation in the cellular response to genotoxic stresses.
source: Moreover, assembly of the PARP1-IKKγ signal complex has been established as a prerequisite for cytoplasmic NF-κB activation in the cellular response to genotoxic stresses (Gibson and Kraus, 2012; McCool and Miyamoto, 2012; Miyamoto, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: PARP1 complexed with IKKγ following CPT treatment in wild-type MEFs.
source: As expected, PARP1 complexed with IKKγ following CPT treatment, whereas there was no detectable PARP1-IKKγ interaction in the absence of genotoxic stress in wild-type MEFs (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The CPT-induced PARP1-IKKγ interaction was abolished in Sam68 KO MEFs.
source: In striking contrast, the CPT-induced PARP1-IKKγ interaction was abolished in Sam68 KO MEFs (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Strong inducible interactions among Sam68, PARP1, and IKKγ were observed in wild-type MEFs at 20 min after CPT treatment.
source: Moreover, strong inducible interactions among Sam68, PARP1, and IKKγ were observed in wild-type MEFs, at 20 min after CPT treatment (Figure 1F–G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F-G.

claim: Immune-depletion of Sam68 using antibodies abolished the CPT-induced PARP1-IKKγ interaction in wild-type MEFs.
source: Of note, immune-depletion of Sam68 using antibodies abolished the CPT-induced PARP1-IKKγ interaction in wild-type MEFs (Figure 1—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: PARP1 interacts with Sam68 and IKKγ simultaneously.
source: suggesting that PARP1 interacts with Sam68 and IKKγ simultaneously.
evidence: This is inferred from the immune-depletion experiment results.

claim: PARP1-mediated PARylation is one of the most crucial post-translational modifications orchestrating DNA damage-initiated NF-κB signaling.
source: Beyond its indispensable role in DNA repair (Gibson and Kraus, 2012), emerging evidence demonstrates that PARP1-mediated PARylation is one of the most crucial post-translational modifications orchestrating DNA damage-initiated NF-κB signaling (Stilmann et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CPT treatment induced a wide array of PARylated proteins peaking at 20 min post stimulation in wild-type MEFs.
source: As expected, CPT treatment induced a wide array of PARylated proteins peaking at 20 min post stimulation in wild-type MEFs, which were diminished by one-hour pretreatment with two independent PARP inhibitors, Olaparib and PJ-34, thus confirming the PAR specificity (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Genotoxic stress-induced PAR synthesis was markedly dampened in Sam68 KO MEFs.
source: Strikingly, genotoxic stress-induced PAR synthesis was markedly dampened in Sam68 KO MEFs (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Genotoxic stress-induced PARylation of PARP1, NBS1, and Ku70 was substantially attenuated in Sam68 KO MEFs.
source: Consistently, genotoxic stress-induced PARylation of the known PARP1 substrates including PARP1 itself, NBS1, and Ku70 was also substantially attenuated in Sam68 KO MEFs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Down-regulation of PARG by siRNA in Sam68 KO MEFs failed to restore CPT-induced PAR production to a similar level to that in wild-type MEFs.
source: However, down-regulation of PARG by siRNA in Sam68 KO MEFs failed to restore CPT-induced PAR production to a similar level to that in wild-type MEFs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The attenuated PAR formation in the absence of Sam68 is not caused by a rapid degradation of PAR chains.
source: which suggests that the attenuated PAR formation in the absence of Sam68 is not caused by a rapid degradation of PAR chains.
evidence: This is inferred from the PARG knockdown experiment results.

claim: CPT and γ-irradiation stimulated PAR production was markedly reduced in primary colonic epithelial cells (CECs) derived from Khdrbs1-/- mice.
source: Furthermore, CPT and γ-irradiation stimulated PAR production was markedly reduced in primary colonic epithelial cells (CECs) derived from Khdrbs1-/- (Sam68 knockout) mice, compared to Khdrbs1+/- (Sam68 heterozygote) controls (Figure 2B–D)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B-D.

claim: Sam68 was enriched in chromatin fractions in MEFs following γ-irradiation.
source: Remarkably, Sam68 was enriched in chromatin fractions in MEFs following γ-irradiation (Figure 2E)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Sam68 was enriched in chromatin fractions in MEFs following CPT treatment.
source: and CPT treatment (Figure 2F)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The kinetics of Sam68 enrichment was similar to that of PARP1 on damaged chromatin.
source: and the kinetics of Sam68 enrichment was similar to that of PARP1 on damaged chromatin (Figure 2F)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Genotoxic stress-induced Sam68 enrichment in chromatin is not dependent on PAR formation.
source: Moreover, Sam68 and PARP1 were still substantially enriched in chromatin fractions in the PARP1-inhibited MEFs following γ-irradiation (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A), indicating that genotoxic stress-induced Sam68 enrichment in chromatin is not dependent on PAR formation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A and inference from the results.

claim: Supplementing exogenous GFP-Sam68 largely restored γ-irradiation-stimulated PAR production in Sam68 KO MEFs.
source: As expected, supplementing exogenous GFP-Sam68, compared to the GFP control, largely restored γ-irradiation-stimulated PAR production in Sam68 KO MEFs (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B.

claim: PARP1 overexpression did not rescue the PAR chain formation in response to γ-irradiation under a Sam68 deleted condition.
source: In contrast, PARP1 overexpression did not rescue the PAR chain formation in response to γ-irradiation under a Sam68 deleted condition (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Sam68 is required for DNA damage-triggered PARP1 activation.
source: which suggests that Sam68 is required for DNA damage-triggered PARP1 activation and is consistent with Sam68 being an essential upstream activator of PARP1.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results showing that PARP1 overexpression cannot rescue PAR formation in Sam68 KO cells.

claim: Sam68 is an essential upstream activator of PARP1.
source: which suggests that Sam68 is required for DNA damage-triggered PARP1 activation and is consistent with Sam68 being an essential upstream activator of PARP1.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results.

claim: PARP1 is the most robust enzyme that catalyzes >90% of PAR formation in cells.
source: DNA-dependent PARP enzymes, i.e. PARP1 and PARP2, are activated during the cellular response to DNA damage, of which PARP1 is the most robust enzyme that catalyzes >90% of PAR formation in cells (Krishnakumar and Kraus, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: No detectable interaction between Sam68 and PARP2 was observed under either unstimulated or damaged conditions.
source: In contrast to the genotoxic stress-induced Sam68-PARP1 interaction (Figure 1F–G and Figure 1—figure supplement 2D), no detectable interaction between Sam68 and PARP2 was observed under either unstimulated or damaged conditions (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Immunoprecipitated PARP1 was associated with Sam68 and various PARylated target proteins in CPT-treated wild-type MEFs.
source: In line with the vigorous PAR production in the presence of genotoxic stress (Figure 2A), immunoprecipitated PARP1 was associated with Sam68 and various PARylated target proteins in CPT-treated wild-type MEFs (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: PARylated species were dramatically reduced in PARP1 immunoprecipitated from Sam68 KO MEFs.
source: In contrast, the PARylated species were dramatically reduced despite an equal amount of PARP1 immunoprecipitated from Sam68 KO MEFs was used (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Supplementing with GFP-tagged Sam68 markedly augmented the DNA damage-triggered PAR synthesis in CPT-treated Sam68 KO MEFs.
source: Conversely, supplementing with GFP-tagged Sam68, in comparison to a GFP control, markedly augmented the DNA damage-triggered PAR synthesis in CPT-treated Sam68 KO MEFs (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B.

claim: DNA damage-activated PARP1 auto-modified itself with the addition of PAR moieties in the presence of NAD+ and DNA.
source: DNA damage-activated PARP1 auto-modified itself with the addition of PAR moieties in the presence of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) and DNA, as indicated by the formation of PARylated PARP1 species (Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 4A) and a corresponding reduction in unmodified PARP1 protein (Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 4B, compare lane 4 with lane 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 4A-B.

claim: Incubation of recombinant Sam68 protein with PARP1 dramatically boosted PAR production.
source: Strikingly, incubation of recombinant Sam68 protein, but not GST control, with PARP1 dramatically boosted PAR production, which was paralleled by a sharp loss of unmodified PARP1 protein (Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 4B, compare lane 5 with lane 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 4B.

claim: Sam68 harbors a stimulatory function for DNA-dependent PARP1 activity.
source: Of note, the amount of Sam68 protein from the boosted PARylation reaction remained at a comparable level (Figure 2H, compare lane 5 with lane 7), thus ruling out the possibility that Sam68 is a substrate of PARP1 in vitro and indicating that Sam68 harbors a stimulatory function for DNA-dependent PARP1 activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results showing that Sam68 levels remain constant while PAR production increases.

claim: Sam68 per se does not possess the enzymatic activity to transfer ADP-ribosyl polymers.
source: In the absence of PARP1, neither GST nor GST-Sam68 protein exhibited PARylation activity (Figure 2H, lanes 1, 2, 6, 7, and 10), indicating that Sam68 per se does not possess the enzymatic activity to transfer ADP-ribosyl polymers.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: In the absence of damaged DNA, incubation of Sam68 and PARP1 failed to form detectable PAR chains from supplemented NAD+.
source: Moreover, in the absence of damaged DNA, incubation of Sam68 and PARP1 failed to form detectable PAR chains from supplemented NAD+ (Figure 2—figure supplement 4C)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4C.

claim: Sam68 stimulates DNA-dependent PARP1 activation and subsequent PAR production.
source: which suggests that Sam68 stimulates DNA-dependent PARP1 activation and subsequent PAR production.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results showing that Sam68 requires damaged DNA to stimulate PARP1.

claim: The full-length, ΔC, and ΔKH truncated Sam68 associate with PARP1.
source: We detected the association of the full-length, ΔC, and ΔKH truncated Sam68 to PARP1, but not GFP control (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Deletion of the N-terminal amino acids 1–102 (ΔN) of Sam68 almost abolished the association of Sam68 to PARP1.
source: In contrast, deletion of the N-terminal amino acids 1–102 (ΔN) of Sam68 almost abolished the association of Sam68 to PARP1 (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The N-terminal residues of Sam68 are critical for the Sam68-PARP1 interaction.
source: suggesting that the N-terminal residues are critical for the Sam68-PARP1 interaction.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results showing that deletion of N-terminus abolishes PARP1 binding.

claim: There is a direct Sam68-PARP1 interaction.
source: Moreover, our pull-down assays using recombinant proteins demonstrated a direct Sam68-PARP1 interaction (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C using recombinant proteins.

claim: ΔN truncated Sam68 protein barely interacted with PARP1.
source: In contrast to the strong association between PARP1 and full-length Sam68, ΔN truncated Sam68 protein barely interacted with PARP1 (Figure 3C)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Transient transfection of full-length Sam68 significantly restored genotoxic stress-induced PARylation in Sam68 KO MEFs.
source: Transient transfection of full-length Sam68, but not GFP control, significantly restored genotoxic stress-induced PARylation (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Transient transfection of full-length Sam68 significantly restored assembly of the PARP1-IKKγ signaling complex in Sam68 KO MEFs.
source: Transient transfection of full-length Sam68, but not GFP control, significantly restored genotoxic stress-induced PARylation (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), assembly of the PARP1-IKKγ signaling complex (Figure 3D)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Transient transfection of full-length Sam68 significantly restored cytoplasmic degradation of IκBα in Sam68 KO MEFs.
source: cytoplasmic degradation of IκBα, and nuclear translocation of p65 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Transient transfection of full-length Sam68 significantly restored nuclear translocation of p65 in Sam68 KO MEFs.
source: cytoplasmic degradation of IκBα, and nuclear translocation of p65 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Full-length Sam68 and Sam68 (ΔN) truncate share strict nuclear localization.
source: In contrast, despite full-length Sam68 and Sam68 (ΔN) truncate sharing strict nuclear localization (Figure 3E)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.
